title: Devarim: small and great alike (Deuteronomy 1:17)
hook: judges must hear the small as the great and fear no one

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devarim from the man who once said he had no words. Your line was words come with time. Today, Moses remembers the judges he appointed.

A desk at a city office, two people in line. One is a well-known developer with a lawyer at his elbow and a building permit worth millions. The other is a retired woman whose neighbor's tree keeps dropping branches on her car. Whose file gets opened first? Whose gets read carefully? It isn't hard to guess how it often goes. Early in his farewell, Moses remembers setting up courts in the wilderness, and the charge he gave the judges. It's about exactly that line at that desk.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE IN LINE.` → `THE BIG FILE AND THE SMALL ONE.` → `MOSES CHARGES THE JUDGES.`

segments.voice: The charge, in the old Jewish translation, says: "ye shall hear the small and the great alike; ye shall not be afraid of the face of any man; for the judgment is God's." Three pieces. First, small and great alike. The rabbis took that literally, about money. In the Talmud, in Sanhedrin, Resh Lakish says a case over a single perutah, a tiny copper coin, must be as precious to the judge as a case over a hundred maneh, a fortune. Same care. Same patience. Same order in the line. Second, don't be afraid of the face of any man. A judge will someday face someone powerful, someone who could ruin them, someone with friends. The verse says: don't look away from the case to look at the face. And the reason is the third piece: the judgment is God's. Read that way, the judge isn't the owner of justice, just the one holding it for a while, and answerable for how it was held. Notice who is listening to this speech. Not judges, mostly. A whole people. Moses is retelling it to everyone, because everyone ends up judging something: whose complaint gets heard at work, which kid's version of the fight gets believed, whose message gets answered tonight and whose waits a week. The small and the great show up at all of those desks.
screen: `HEAR THE SMALL AND THE GREAT ALIKE.` · `A PENNY CASE, A FORTUNE CASE.` · `DON'T FEAR ANY FACE.` · `THE JUDGMENT IS GOD'S.` · then, large: `SMALL AND GREAT ALIKE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a small worry someone brought you lately that you brushed past: a kid's question, a coworker's minor complaint, a parent's repeated story. Hold it up the way you'd hold a big one, and ask what they were really asking for. Let yourself feel the size it was to them.
Devarim. Words, the name of this last book, where Moses retells even the charge he gave the first judges.
Your line: small and great alike. A week of edges: a date remembered, a city of refuge, a land that's shared, the edge of the Jordan, and now the words. That's day four hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Jewish law holds judges to equal care for every case regardless of its value or the parties' standing, and the Talmud's rule that a penny case is as precious as a fortune is still cited in teaching about Jewish courts.

match.prompt: inside the judges' charge — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: you're a judge. one case is over a single copper coin, the other over a fortune, and the rich man is impatient. what does the Talmud say?
options: hear the fortune first; it matters more.

fork.reveal: Sanhedrin reads small and great alike as a penny case being as precious as a case over a hundred maneh.

chat.meaning: Moses tells the judges' charge to the whole people: hear small and great alike, because everyone ends up judging something.

maneh.meaning: a unit of money; a hundred maneh is a fortune
